Construct a Pooling Design Matrix by Family

Source: R/pool_matrix.R
PoolMatrix.Rd

Dispatch to one of the existing pooling-design constructors in ppgt using a user-facing family label. The function is a convenience wrapper over the package's structured constructors and returns only the pooling matrix \(\mathbf{M}\). It does not claim that \(d\) alone uniquely determines a pooling matrix across design families.

Usage

PoolMatrix(
  family = c("pp", "pbest", "hyper", "separable", "disjunct", "dorfman", "array", "bibd",
    "hypercube", "kirkman", "pg"),
  d = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  q = NULL,
  J = NULL,
  method = NULL,
  verify = TRUE,
  seed = NULL,
  ...,
  verbose = FALSE
)

Arguments

family

Character scalar selecting the constructor family. Supported values are "pp", "pbest", "hyper", "separable", "disjunct", "dorfman", "array", "bibd", "hypercube", "kirkman", and "pg".

d

Optional integer scalar. This argument is passed only to families for which \(d\) is a native parameter, such as Polynomial Pools, separable designs, disjunct designs, and hypercube designs. For other families it is ignored unless explicitly documented for the selected constructor.

N

Optional integer scalar giving the number of individuals. When the selected family uses \(N\) directly, this value is forwarded to the underlying constructor. For design families whose native interface uses a different symbol such as \(v\), PoolMatrix() uses N only as a convenience alias when that mapping is exact.

q

Optional integer scalar. This argument is forwarded only to families where \(q\) is a native parameter, such as Polynomial Pools, HYPER, hypercube designs, and projective-plane designs.

J

Optional integer scalar giving the requested number of pools. This is forwarded only to families where the native constructor accepts a free row-count argument. For Polynomial Pools, J may be used only to infer \(n_l = J/q\) when that ratio is an integer.

method

Optional character scalar giving a family-specific construction mode. Examples include "pp" or "clinical" for family = "pbest", "auto", "random", or "reed-solomon" for family = "separable" and family = "disjunct", and "2d" or "3d" for family = "array".

verify

Logical scalar. This is forwarded to families that expose an explicit verification option, namely "separable" and "disjunct".

seed

Optional integer scalar. This is forwarded only to families whose current constructor uses randomness, such as random separable/disjunct designs and the package-specific clinical P-BEST helper.

...

Additional family-specific arguments. Supported names are:

nl

Number of PP layers for family = "pp" or the PP-based "pbest" path.

reorder

Logical reorder flag for family = "hyper".

g

Pool size for family = "dorfman".

r, c

Grid dimensions for the two-dimensional array path.

d1, d2, d3

Grid dimensions for the three-dimensional array path.

v, k, lambda

BIBD or Kirkman parameters.

verbose

Logical scalar; if TRUE, emit a short message describing the chosen dispatch path.

Value

A binary pooling matrix returned by the selected constructor, usually of class dgCMatrix. The matrix is returned directly, and carries an additional "poolmatrix" attribute containing the selected family, dispatch method, and the key arguments used by the wrapper. The return value is the stage-1 design matrix \(\mathbf{M}\) only.

Details

Let \(\mathbf{M} \in \{0,1\}^{J \times N}\) denote a pooling design matrix, where \(J\) is the number of pools and \(N\) is the number of individuals. The wrapper PoolMatrix() is a constructor-only dispatcher over existing matrix constructors. It returns \(\mathbf{M}\) and stops there. In particular, it does not handle adaptive versus non-adaptive workflow selection, retesting scenarios, stage-2 protocol logic, or decoder behavior. Those concerns belong in separate functions or in package documentation, not in this wrapper.

The function also does not solve a universal inverse problem of the form "given \(d\), construct the unique matrix." The symbol \(d\) has different meanings across the supported families, and some families do not use \(d\) at all.

The dispatch rules are:

family = "pp"

Dispatch to pp_matrix using \(q\), \(d\), \(n_l\), and optional \(N\).

family = "pbest"

Dispatch either to the standard PP-based 48-pool family through pp_matrix with \((q,d,n_l,N) = (8,3,6,384)\), or to the package-specific clinical helper pbest_clinical_matrix when method = "clinical".

family = "hyper"

Dispatch to hyper_matrix using \(N\), \(J\), and \(q\).

family = "separable"

Dispatch to SeparableMatrix using \(N\), \(d\), optional \(J\), and the selected method.

family = "disjunct"

Dispatch to DisjunctMatrix using \(N\), \(d\), optional \(J\), and the selected method.

family = "dorfman"

Dispatch to dorfman_matrix using \(N\) and the explicit pool-size argument g.

family = "array"

Dispatch to array_matrix or array_matrix_3d according to method.

family = "bibd"

Dispatch to bibd_matrix using \(v\), \(k\), and \(\lambda\).

family = "hypercube"

Dispatch to hypercube_matrix using \(q\) and \(d\).

family = "kirkman"

Dispatch to kirkman_matrix using \(v\).

family = "pg"

Dispatch to pg_matrix using \(q\).

Family-specific parameters remain explicit. In particular, the wrapper does not impose \(d\)-only semantics on families such as HYPER, Dorfman, array, BIBD, Kirkman, or projective-plane designs, where \(d\) is not the native defining parameter. Likewise, calling PoolMatrix() should be read only as "construct \(\mathbf{M}\) for the chosen family" and not as "run the complete testing workflow" for that family.

References

Tan, Y. H. I. (2020). Pooling matrix designs for group testing. SIAM Undergraduate Research Online, 13, 1-21.

Shental, N., Levy, S., Wuvshet, V., et al. (2020). Efficient high-throughput SARS-CoV-2 testing to detect asymptomatic carriers. Science Advances, 6(37), eabc5961.

Hong, F. S., Shah, N., Briggs, A., et al. (2022). HYPER group testing for SARS-CoV-2: A flexible, easy-to-implement, and highly efficient method. Nature Communications, 13, Article 3626.

D'yachkov, A. G., & Rykov, V. V. (1982). Bounds on the length of disjunctive codes. Problemy Peredachi Informatsii, 18(3), 7-13.

Dorfman, R. (1943). The detection of defective members of large populations. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 14(4), 436-440.
